mainEntity.name: Can I use whitening toothpaste on composite bonding?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is generally not advisable to use whitening toothpastes on composite bonding. Many whitening toothpastes contain abrasive particles or low concentrations of hydrogen peroxide designed to act on natural tooth enamel. These agents do not change the colour of composite resin, but they can gradually abrade and roughen the surface, making the material more susceptible to picking up future stains. A low-abrasivity fluoride toothpaste is the safer, more appropriate choice for daily use on bonded teeth. Your dentist or hygienist can recommend a suitable product if you are unsure.

mainEntity.name: How long does composite bonding last before it needs replacing?

acceptedAnswer.text: The lifespan of composite bonding varies between patients and depends on a range of factors including oral hygiene, diet, bite force, and how well the bonding is maintained. On average, composite bonding may last anywhere from four to eight years before replacement or significant repair is needed, though some patients may experience longer-lasting results with careful maintenance — individual outcomes vary. Regular dental check-ups allow your dentist to monitor the condition of your bonding and advise on appropriate timing for any maintenance or replacement.

mainEntity.name: Will professional tooth whitening affect my composite bonding?

acceptedAnswer.text: Professional tooth whitening treatments — whether in-clinic or home-based — are designed to lighten natural tooth enamel and do not change the colour of composite resin. This means that if you whiten your natural teeth, the composite bonding may no longer match, potentially creating a visible colour difference. If you are considering whitening, it is important to discuss this with your dentist first, particularly if you have composite bonding. Your dentist can advise on the best sequence or approach for your individual situation.

mainEntity.name: Is it safe to have a hygiene clean with composite bonding?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, it is safe to have professional hygiene appointments when you have composite bonding, but it is important to inform your hygienist about your restorations. They can adapt their cleaning approach to use instruments and materials that are safe for composite surfaces. Some hygienists offer air polishing protocols specifically designed for use around composite restorations. Routine hygiene appointments are actually an important part of maintaining composite bonding, helping to keep the surface clean and minimise staining.

mainEntity.name: Why has the edge of my bonding gone dark?

acceptedAnswer.text: Darkening at the margins (edges) of composite bonding where it meets the natural tooth is a relatively common occurrence over time. It can result from staining pigment working into a small gap at the margin, from marginal breakdown of the material, or from staining along the bonded edge itself. In some cases it can be addressed with professional polishing; in others, the margin may need to be repaired or resealed by a dentist. If you notice this, it is worth mentioning at your next dental appointment so that your dentist can assess it directly.

mainEntity.name: Can I eat normally after composite bonding?

acceptedAnswer.text: After the initial period following placement — usually 24 to 48 hours, during which very hard or very staining foods are often best avoided — most patients can return to a normal diet. Over the longer term, composite bonding is functional for everyday eating, though very hard foods (such as biting into whole apples or crunching ice) and habits such as nail biting or chewing pens can increase the risk of chipping. Your dentist will advise you on any specific post-treatment guidance relevant to your individual situation.
